## The idea

An interval is not heard the same way in every presentation. Two successive notes create motion with a direction and a destination. The same two pitches struck together create a colour whose cues may include fusion, beating, and roughness. Familiarity with one form does not automatically produce recognition of the other.

Keep separate descriptions for melodic and harmonic intervals for that reason. A personal phrase such as “small, tense step” or “open, fused span” can become a useful retrieval cue if it points to something you consistently hear. The description should remain attached to a register, direction, and sound source until you know which part of it transfers.

The program introduces four distances in a fixed order. It plays each as an ascending motion, pauses, then presents both pitches together. The standard name appears after both presentations, leaving time to form your own observation first.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 68
use_synth :piano

intervals = {1 => "minor second", 4 => "major third", 7 => "perfect fifth", 12 => "octave"}
root = note(:c4)

intervals.each do |distance, label|
  play root, release: 0.7
  sleep 1
  play root + distance, release: 0.7
  sleep 2

  play root, release: 2
  play root + distance, release: 2
  sleep 3
  puts "#{distance} semitones: #{label}"
end
```

In the melodic presentation, follow the size and direction of the leap from C. In the harmonic presentation, stop following a path and attend to the combined sound. The minor second should retain much more close motion than the octave; the fifth often feels open without fusing as completely as the octave. These descriptions are starting points to test, not definitions supplied by the code.

## Change one thing

1. Reverse every melodic interval while leaving the harmonic pairs unchanged. Descending motion may call up a different contour or emotional association even though the absolute semitone distance remains fixed.

2. Restore the ascending forms and move the root from C4 to F-sharp3. The intervals retain their distances, but the new register and pitch context alter their surface colour. Mark which cues survive the move.

3. Restore C4 and use a sine synth for harmonic pairs while retaining piano for melodic forms. Sines expose beating and fusion; piano attacks can make the two successive events easier to locate. Do not compare smoothness without noting the timbre change.

## Why it works

The dictionary maps a numerical distance to more than a standard label. Each entry can carry an ascending description, a descending description, a harmonic description, and an optional remembered tune. Those fields are observations about presentations of the interval, not alternate definitions of it.

Begin with a narrow fixed set because comparison builds the categories. A minor second becomes clearer beside a major third; a fifth can be contrasted with an octave. Show the label soon after both presentations during this reference work so the sound and name remain paired. Random order becomes useful later, when you want to test retrieval instead of building the association.

Vary root and register only after the first four distances have distinct descriptions. If every major third is C4–E4, you may learn that pair of pitches rather than the relation between them. Transposition tests whether the distance survives when the familiar absolute notes disappear. A wider range also exposes which descriptors belonged to one register.

Tune anchors can help, but they contain hidden assumptions. A remembered excerpt may begin with a pickup, embellish the target, or place the cue between different scale degrees than you recall. Store the exact two notes and direction that form the anchor. If it repeatedly produces a wrong answer, remove it rather than defending the association.

Personal adjectives need the same discipline. “Wide” may distinguish an octave from a second, but it says little about a fifth beside a sixth. “Beating” depends on timbre and register. “Settled” may reflect tonal context rather than distance alone. Keep a description when it directs attention to a reproducible cue and revise it when varied prompts expose its limits.

The log provides labels and distances; playback provides the evidence for your descriptions. Lesson 20 turns this reference material into a prompt, answer interval, and delayed reveal. That change in control flow marks the difference between studying a sound and testing whether you can retrieve its name.

## Take it further

Create a personal reference hash whose possible keys run from 0 through 12 semitones. Each completed entry should contain the standard label, an ascending melodic description, a descending melodic description, a harmonic description, and an optional tune anchor with its exact cue notes.

Complete four entries first. Audition all their presentations in Sonic Pi 5, revise descriptions that fail to point toward a repeatable feature, and then test the set in mixed order. Add one new interval only after identifying nine of ten prompts in two consecutive sessions. A small dictionary with specific evidence is more useful than twelve entries copied from someone else's adjectives.
